summary: A Best Current Practice with examples of Session Initiation Protocol services, covering most features of IP Centrex and PBX offerings. Most services are done in SIP user agents, although some need a SIP proxy or extensions such as REFER, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. It gives examples of call flows for these features.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP is the protocol that sets up internet phone calls. This document shows how 18 office phone features, such as hold, transfer and forwarding, are built from SIP messages. For each feature it lists the messages the phones send, in order, and the extra header fields some of them carry.

questions: how does sip attended transfer work
how does sip call hold work
subtitle: Worked call flows for 18 office phone services, showing the SIP messages that each one sends.

tldr.problem: Businesses expect IP phones to offer the features of a PBX or an IP Centrex service, such as hold, transfer, forwarding and call pickup, but SIP itself defines only the building blocks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through 18 services message by message, naming the SIP methods, header fields and extensions each one uses, among them REFER, Replaces, Join, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY.
tldr.outcome: It is a companion to the SIP specifications, not a protocol of its own: it shows one working way to build each service and says other approaches, such as 3pcc or back-to-back user agents, are not excluded.

today: RFC 5359 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 144) published in October 2008, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to the SIP specifications, which remain definitive for protocol questions, and its examples are meant to be read alongside them.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5359 gives worked examples of 18 SIP services, the kind of features an office phone system offers. The list includes call hold, consultation hold, music on hold, three kinds of transfer, three kinds of call forwarding, two kinds of three-way conference, find-me, incoming and outgoing call screening, call park, call pickup, automatic redial and click to dial. The single line extension flow was removed from the document and is covered separately.

The flows were developed while a SIP network was being designed, and they stand as an example set of IP Centrex services, where a carrier supplies the phone system, or of PBX (private branch exchange) services inside one organisation. The authors hope the document will be useful to implementers, designers and protocol researchers alike, and will help further the goal of a standard implementation of RFC 3261 and some of its extensions. The flows are described as carefully checked and working group reviewed scenarios, presented as a companion to the specifications.

The SIP specification and the other referenced documents are definitive as far as protocol issues are concerned. These flows are not the only way to implement the services: other approaches, such as 3pcc (Third Party Call Control) in RFC 3725 or back-to-back user agents, can be used, and this specification does not preclude them. The peer-to-peer design and principles behind these examples are described in the Multiparty Framework document.
sections.plainLanguage: This document shows how 18 office phone features, such as hold, transfer and forwarding, are built from SIP messages. For each feature it lists the messages the phones send, in order, and the extra header fields some of them carry. It is a companion to the SIP specifications, not a new protocol.

sections.title: How the Flows Are Drawn and Written
sections.content:
Every example in the document has the same three parts: a textual description of the scenario, a message flow diagram showing the messages exchanged between separate network elements, and the detailed contents of each message shown in the diagram. Messages are identified in the figures as F1, F2 and so on, and each identifier points to the matching entry in the message details that follows.

In the diagrams, dashed lines represent control messages that are mandatory for the call scenario, and double dashed lines represent media paths between network elements. A message name in parentheses marks an optional control message. The document also explains its own shorthand: lines longer than 72 characters are handled using the <allOneLine> convention defined in RFC 4475, and comments inside the message details are written between /* and */.

The examples are simplified so that the document can be read and edited. The HTTP Digest responses are not actual MD5 encodings, Call-IDs are often repeated, CSeq counts often begin at 1, header fields are usually shown in the same order, only the minimum required header field set is shown, and message body content lengths are often written as ... where the real octet count would be.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example gives a short story, a diagram of the messages, and the full text of every message. In the diagrams, double lines show where the audio travels, and a message name in parentheses marks an optional message. The message text is deliberately simplified, so the values in it are not the ones a real phone would send.

sections.title: Call Hold, Consultation Hold and Music on Hold
sections.content:
In the call hold example, Alice calls Bob, Bob puts the call on hold, takes it off hold, and Alice then hangs up. Hold is unidirectional in nature, so the user agent that places the other party on hold will generally also stop sending media, which results in no media exchange between the two user agents. Older user agents may set the connection address to 0.0.0.0 when initiating hold, but the document notes that this behaviour has been deprecated in favour of the a=inactive SDP attribute if no media is sent, or the a=sendonly attribute if media is still sent.

Bob starts the hold by sending an INVITE inside the dialog that already exists, with the same Call-ID as the original invitation. That request carries the rendering feature tag defined in RFC 4235 as a parameter on the Contact header field, to indicate that Bob's user agent is no longer rendering media to Bob. The SDP body of the request sets the media direction to a=sendonly. The dialog is not torn down, so the same two user agents stay connected for the whole call.

Consultation hold adds a third party. Bob holds Alice, calls Carol, disconnects from Carol, and then takes Alice off hold. The hold and off-hold steps use the same re-INVITE pattern as plain hold.

For music on hold, Bob sends a REFER to a music server. The music server sends its own INVITE to Alice with a Replaces header field, so the session with Alice moves from Bob to the music server, and the server then sends RTP audio to Alice. Bob takes Alice back by sending an INVITE with Replaces to Alice. The music server advertises the automaton feature tag from RFC 3840 and the byeless feature tag from RFC 4235 to describe its capabilities. If Alice does not wish to receive music on hold, her user agent can refuse that INVITE, and she remains on hold with Bob, but in silence.
sections.plainLanguage: Holding a call does not end it. Bob's phone sends a new INVITE in the conversation that is already running, marks itself as no longer playing sound, and the two phones stop exchanging audio. To play music instead, Bob asks a music server to take the call over with a REFER, and the server's own call to Alice replaces Bob's.

sections.title: Transferring a Call to Someone Else
sections.content:
Three transfer examples cover the common cases, and all of them use the REFER method from RFC 3515. The person transferring the call sends a REFER whose Refer-To header field names the other party, and the user agent on the other end then makes the new call itself.

In the unattended transfer, Alice calls Bob and then transfers him to Carol. Alice sends the REFER, Bob answers with 202 Accepted, and Bob sends a NOTIFY to report the progress of the transfer. Alice then sends a BYE, which ends the media but not the dialog: the dialog between Alice and Bob still exists until the subscription created by the REFER has terminated, either because of a NOTIFY containing a Subscription-State: terminated;reason=noresource header field, as in the final NOTIFY, or because of a 481 response to a NOTIFY. Bob sets up the session with Carol and reports the success of the transfer back to Alice. If the transfer fails, Bob can send a new INVITE back to Alice to re-establish the session.

In the attended transfer, Bob holds Alice, calls Carol to announce the transfer, places Carol on hold, and then transfers Alice to Carol. The new session replaces the session between Bob and Carol. The Refer-To URI that Bob sends is the Contact URI that Carol returned in her 200 OK, with the Replaces header field from RFC 3891 inserted into it, so that only the correct instance of Carol is reached. The gr URI parameter on that Contact URI indicates that it is a GRUU, an address that stays globally routable outside the dialog. Without knowing that the Contact URI is a GRUU, Bob must be prepared to retry the REFER with a Refer-To URI of the URI used to reach Carol, but with a Require: replaces header escaped into the Refer-To header field.

The third example transfers the call with an instant message. Bob sends Carol a SIP MESSAGE, the extension for instant messaging defined in RFC 3428, that contains Alice's URI and an embedded Replaces header field. If Carol clicks on the URI, her SIP user agent sends an INVITE to Alice that replaces the session with Bob. The document notes that another instant messaging protocol, or another method, could have been used to pass the URI from Bob to Carol.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer hands the call to a third person with a REFER message. The phone on the other end then makes the new call and reports what happened back to the person who transferred it. The attended version checks with the third person first, and the instant message version sends the address in a message instead of a call.

sections.title: Forwarding a Call and Finding a User
sections.content:
Three forwarding examples show what a proxy does when a call should go somewhere else. In the unconditional example, Bob wants all calls forwarded to the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), which is just another URI to the proxy server. Alice calls Bob, and the proxy server rewrites the Request URI and forwards the INVITE to a gateway. The 181 Call Is Being Forwarded response is shown as sent by the proxy, and the document notes that strictly speaking the proxy is behaving as a user agent in this case, as a proxy cannot generate non-100 provisional responses. Forwarding could also be accomplished using a redirect, a 302 Moved Temporarily response.

In the forwarding on busy example, calls to B1 are to be forwarded to B2 if B1 is busy, and the proxy knows B1 is busy because B1 answers the INVITE with 486 Busy Here. The proxy server then places the call to B2. In the forwarding on no answer example, the proxy sends the INVITE to B1, waits, gives up when the request times out, cancels the pending request with a CANCEL, and receives 487. It then forwards the call to B2.

The find-me example in section 2.12 locates a person rather than a single number. A call to Bob results in an attempt to locate Bob by calling locations from a list of contacts. In the diagram the proxy tries B1 first and the request times out, then tries B2, which answers 480 Not Logged In, then tries B3, which answers 486 Busy Here, and finally reaches B4, which rings and answers. The location that answers the call becomes the active set, and no other sets may join the call. The document notes that the flow shows a sequential search, and that the search could be accomplished using parallel forking.
sections.plainLanguage: When a call should go elsewhere, the proxy changes the address on the invitation and sends it on. It can do that for every call, only when the person is busy, or only when nobody answers. The find-me example goes further and tries a list of places, one after another, until someone picks up.

sections.title: Three-Way Conference Calls
sections.content:
Two examples show how three people end up in one call. In the first, Alice and Bob are in a two-party call and Bob wants to add Carol. Bob is capable of media mixing in a three-party call, so he first sends Alice a re-INVITE that changes his Contact URIs to one that indicates Bob's mixer and acts like a focus. As a result, Bob includes the isfocus feature tag from RFC 3840, as described in RFC 4579. Bob then INVITEs Carol using the same Contact URI. The document notes that Bob could wait to re-INVITE Alice until after Carol has answered, and that he could also put Alice on hold before calling Carol.

In the second example, Carol wants to join a call she is not yet part of. She may have learned Bob's dialog identifier using some non-SIP means, or possibly from a NOTIFY with the dialog package sent by Bob. Carol sends Bob an INVITE containing a Join header field, defined in RFC 3911, that identifies the dialog between Alice and Bob. The header field names that dialog by Call-ID and by the From and To tags, in the form Join: 12345600@atlanta.example.com;from-tag=1234567;to-tag=23431. Bob re-INVITEs Alice to switch to focus mode and includes the isfocus feature tag, then accepts the INVITE from Carol, resulting in the three-way call.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference call needs one phone to mix the voices and act as the focus. In one example the person already in the call invites a third person in. In the other, the third person asks to join by naming the existing call, and the phone in the call accepts and switches to focus mode.

sections.title: Screening Incoming and Outgoing Calls
sections.content:
Incoming call screening works from a list of addresses a person does not want to hear from. Bob has such a list and Alice is included on it. Alice attempts to call Bob, and the first three messages show that Bob does not accept INVITEs that have not been screened by the proxy: Bob answers Alice's INVITE with 305 Use Proxy, and Alice's user agent then sends the INVITE to the proxy instead. The proxy challenges Alice with 407 Proxy Authentication Required and, once she is authenticated, refuses the call with 403 Screening Failure (Terminating). The document is explicit that call screening cannot be done using the From header field, so some form of authentication credentials must be used.

The refusal carries an announcement URI in an Error-Info header field, which Alice accesses by sending an INVITE to listen to the announcement. The announcement server uses the automaton and rendering feature tags to indicate that it is a media server only capable of playing announcements.

Outgoing call screening is the mirror image. Alice has a list of addresses to which she will not be able to place a call, and Bob is included on it. The proxy challenges her with 407 Proxy Authentication Required and then refuses with 403 Screening Failure (Originating). Alice can establish a session to listen to the announcement in the Error-Info header field, in the same way as in the incoming case.
sections.plainLanguage: A screening list blocks calls in one direction. For incoming calls, the phone only accepts calls the proxy has checked, and the proxy refuses the call when the caller is on the list. For outgoing calls, the proxy refuses the call when the number is on the list. Either way the caller is given the address of a recorded announcement that they can listen to.

sections.title: Parking a Call and Picking It Up
sections.content:
Call park is a special case of transfer. Alice calls Bob, and Bob parks the call at a park server by sending the server a REFER. The park server sends an INVITE to Alice with a Replaces header field, which replaces the session between Alice and Bob, and it uses the automaton, rendering and byeless feature tags to indicate its capabilities to Alice. The call is accepted by Alice, so Alice sends a BYE to Bob. Bob receives notification of the successful park, and he also receives the dialog identifiers in the application/sip body of the NOTIFY response. The document notes that this call flow could also be used for music on hold.

To retrieve the call, Carol needs those dialog identifiers, and she obtains them from a NOTIFY from the park server. In the diagram she first sends a SUBSCRIBE to the park server, receives the NOTIFY, and then sends an INVITE containing the dialog identifiers to Alice. That INVITE replaces the session with the park server. Alice accepts the call and sends a BYE to the park server, and the media from the server stops.

Call pickup answers a call for someone else. Bob and Bill are part of a work group at example.com that can pick up each other's calls. Alice calls Bob, who does not answer, and Bill wishes to pick up the call. Bill sends a SUBSCRIBE to Bob to retrieve the dialog information, and then generates an INVITE with a Replaces to Alice. Alice answers the INVITE and sends a CANCEL to Bob, which stops Bob's phone from ringing. The document notes that the relative order of the 487 response, its ACK and the 200 OK to the CANCEL is not deterministic. The Replaces header field in this example carries the early-only parameter, which prevents Alice from accepting the INVITE if Bob has already accepted the INVITE; if Bill had wished to take the call from Bob regardless of whether he had answered, the parameter would not have been present. The subscription between the two colleagues could also have been established prior to Alice's call.
sections.plainLanguage: Parking leaves a call at a server so that someone else can collect it later. The phone that parked it receives the details of the parked call, and the colleague who collects it puts those details into a new invitation that takes the call over. Pickup is simpler: a colleague answers a call that is already ringing for someone else.

sections.title: Automatic Redial and Click to Dial
sections.content:
Automatic redial covers the case where the person called is busy. Bob is initially busy when Alice calls, and Alice receives 486 Busy Here. Alice subscribes to Bob's call state with a SUBSCRIBE request, and Bob sends a NOTIFY when he is available. Alice is alerted, and she then sends an INVITE to Bob to establish the session. The subscription is terminated with a further SUBSCRIBE once the call is over.

Click to dial starts a call from somewhere other than a phone. While browsing the web on his PC, Bob clicks on Carol's SIP URI, intending to establish a session with Carol. Bob's web browser passes the SIP URI to the SIP client on Bob's PC, and the PC client is configured with the URI of Bob's SIP phone. A REFER is sent to that phone, which results in the establishment of the session between Bob and Carol. Bob's PC requests that no REFER dialog be established by the use of the Refer-Sub: false header field, defined in RFC 4488. The document prefers this flow to the 3pcc flow because the end-to-end SIP signaling is not interrupted by the 3pcc controller, and because Bob's experience of the call will not be marred by the lack of ringback tone or possible clipping. Suitable authorization of the REFER and explicit authorization of the triggered INVITE by Bob are necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Automatic redial waits for the busy person to become free and then calls again. Click to dial does the opposite: it starts a call from a link on a web page. The program on the computer asks the phone to make the call, so the call runs from the phone to the other person as usual.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since many of the examples in this document involve SIP call control, either peer-to-peer or 3pcc, the security considerations in the Multiparty Framework document apply.

Many of the services shown also rely on a particular user agent being part of a group. Members of a group could be, for example, employees within a particular department, a set of home phone extensions, or members of a call centre. User agents that are part of the group permit other group members special privileges and features. A user agent may not in general allow another user agent to learn detailed dialog information, but this information might be shared with another group member in order to facilitate a service such as call pickup. Group members must be authenticated using normal SIP means such as certificates or shared secrets.

The service examples make extensive use of the SIP call control primitives REFER, Replaces, Join and the dialog package, so the security considerations associated with each of those extensions, in RFC 3515, RFC 3891, RFC 3911 and RFC 4235, apply to the scenarios in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these features only work between phones that belong to the same group, such as the people in one department. A phone in the group may share call details with another member of the group, which it would refuse to do with anyone else. So each member has to prove who it is, with a certificate or a shared secret.

items.title: Hold
items.text: Put a call on hold and take it off hold again, with the session kept open.

items.title: Transfer
items.text: Hand the call to a third person with a REFER request.

items.title: Forwarding
items.text: Let the proxy send the call on: always, when busy, or when unanswered.

items.title: Conferencing
items.text: Bring a third person into a call, by invitation or by request.

items.title: Screening
items.text: Block calls in one direction using a list of addresses.

items.title: Park and pickup
items.text: Leave a call at a server for a colleague, or answer for a colleague.

items.title: Redial and click to dial
items.text: Wait until a busy person frees up, or start a call from a web page.
